TITLE


AI Literacy in Applied Contexts: When the AI Tells You What to Do


DESCRIPTION (100 words)


Most AI literacy pedagogy was built for one scenario: a student prompts a model, receives text, and shapes the output. That is the compositional case. It does not describe what nurses, coders, mechanics, or agricultural technicians encounter. For these practitioners, AI is embedded infrastructure that recommends an action. The cognitive demand is not revision — it is judgment at the moment of deployment. The failure modes are different: automation bias, fixation, anchoring, perseveration. This session introduces a framework for AI literacy in directive contexts, identifies the specific cognitive errors practitioners are most likely to make, and argues that literacy emerges through practice, not instruction.


25-WORD DRAFT


AI literacy was built for the wrong context. When AI tells you what to do, writing skills don’t protect you. Judgment does.


100-WORD DRAFT


Most AI literacy frameworks assume you’re writing with AI — prompting, revising, arguing. That’s not what HIMA professionals do. You encounter AI as embedded infrastructure that recommends a code, flags a record, surfaces a risk. The cognitive demand isn’t revision. It’s judgment under pressure. The failure modes are different: automation bias, fixation, overtrust, anchoring. The research literature barely covers this. The pedagogy doesn’t exist yet. This session introduces a framework for directive AI contexts — and argues that what healthcare professionals need isn’t more AI instruction. It’s repeated practice in realistic scenarios where the cost of getting it wrong is real.


400-WORD DRAFT


I want to start by asking you two questions. The first: how transformative do you think AI will be — for healthcare, for the world? The second: how concerned are you about the long-term risks? High transformation, low risk. High transformation, high risk. Low transformation, low risk. Low transformation, high risk. Four different positions. All of them are partly right.


Here’s what I find interesting. Most AI literacy in higher education — and most guidance organizations are giving to professionals right now — assumes you’re in the first category. That you’re using AI as a writing partner. You prompt a model, you get text back, you revise it. The evidence of your thinking is in the conversation. The artifact is the document you produce.


That is the compositional case. It doesn’t describe your work.


What HIMA professionals encounter is different. The AI is embedded in your workflow before you sit down. It has already recommended a code, flagged a discrepancy, suggested a DRG. You arrive at the output, not the conversation. And the cognitive demand isn’t revision — it’s a judgment call in the space between what the system said and what you sign.


That distinction matters because the failure modes are different. In compositional contexts — academic writing, legal drafting, business analysis — the main cognitive risk is delegation: you stop revising and accept the first draft. Recoverable. In directive contexts — coding, nursing, manufacturing — the risks are automation bias, fixation, anchoring, and what I call perseveration: continuing down the path the AI established even when the patient, the record, or the situation is telling you something else.


The research literature has almost nothing on pedagogy for directive contexts. The frameworks are built for the compositional case.


What that means practically: the habits that protect an academic writer using AI don’t protect a coder using AI. A coder needs to practice the moment of pause before acting. Needs to have validated and verified so many times under realistic conditions that it becomes automatic. Needs to know what fixation looks like from the inside — attention locked on the AI-flagged code while the complication hiding two lines up goes unread.


Literacy, in directive contexts, isn’t knowing about AI. It’s a practiced habit of judgment. And it emerges through repetition, not instruction.


That’s what I want to talk about today.

This is substantially stronger than most “AI literacy” abstracts because it identifies a real category error in current pedagogy rather than just advocating “more critical thinking.” The core distinction — compositional vs directive AI contexts — is the contribution. That framing is clear, portable, and likely publishable if developed carefully.


A few things to tighten:


“The research literature barely covers this” is directionally true, but overstated as written. There is adjacent literature in:


clinical decision support,

aviation automation,

human factors,

cognitive systems engineering,

alarm fatigue,

automation bias research.


Your claim is stronger if you say the AI literacy literature specifically underdevelops directive contexts, rather than implying nobody has studied these phenomena.

“Perseveration” is interesting but potentially risky terminology. In neuropsychology it has a specific meaning. You can still use it, but define it crisply or consider “trajectory lock-in” or “path dependence after AI suggestion.” Otherwise some audiences may think you are borrowing a clinical term too loosely.

The best sentence in the entire set is probably:

“You arrive at the output, not the conversation.”

That is the conceptual pivot.

The weakest phrase is probably “the cost of getting it wrong is real.” It sounds generic. You can be more concrete.


What I would change structurally


The 400-word version currently spends too long on the transformation/risk quadrant opening. It’s rhetorically familiar territory and delays the actual thesis. Your strongest material begins at:

“That is the compositional case. It doesn’t describe your work.”

I would move toward the distinction faster.


Suggested revision of the 100-word version


This keeps your argument but sharpens the claims and reduces overstatement.

Most AI literacy frameworks assume people are writing with AI: prompting, revising, evaluating generated text. That is the compositional case. It is not the environment most healthcare information professionals work in. In practice, AI often appears as embedded infrastructure that recommends a code, flags a discrepancy, or prioritizes a risk. The cognitive demand is not composition but judgment under deployment conditions. The dominant failure modes change accordingly: automation bias, anchoring, fixation, and overtrust. This session introduces a framework for directive AI contexts and argues that AI literacy in these settings emerges less from instruction than from repeated practice under realistic conditions.

Suggested revision of the 25-word version


Your current one is good, but “writing skills don’t protect you” is slightly too dismissive and invites unnecessary pushback.


A tighter version:

AI literacy was built for the wrong context. When AI recommends action, the critical skill is not prompting. It is judgment under pressure.

Or even more compressed:

Most AI literacy assumes you write with AI. Healthcare professionals act on AI recommendations. The relevant skill is judgment, not composition.

Most important conceptual refinement


Right now you are implicitly arguing there are two epistemic relationships with AI:

Context
Human role
Primary risk
Literacy requirement
Compositional
Author/editor
Delegation
Revision and verification
Directive
Decision-maker/operator
Automation bias
Situated judgment

That table — literally or conceptually — is probably the backbone of the talk.


Because once you define the distinction clearly, everything else follows:


different cognition,

different pedagogy,

different assessment,

different training environments,

different ethical failures.


That is the real argument.

TITLE


AI Literacy in Applied Contexts: When the AI Tells You What to Do


DESCRIPTION (100 words)


Most AI literacy frameworks assume people are writing with AI: prompting, revising, evaluating generated text. That is the compositional case. It is not the environment most healthcare information professionals work in. In practice, AI often appears as embedded infrastructure that recommends a code, flags a discrepancy, or prioritizes a risk. The cognitive demand is not composition but judgment under deployment conditions. The dominant failure modes change accordingly: automation bias, anchoring, fixation, and overtrust. This session introduces a framework for directive AI contexts and argues that AI literacy in these settings emerges less from instruction than from repeated practice under realistic conditions.


25-WORD DRAFT


AI literacy was built for the wrong context. When AI recommends action, prompting skills don’t protect you. The critical skill is judgment under pressure.


100-WORD DRAFT


Most AI literacy frameworks assume you’re writing with AI — prompting, revising, arguing. That’s not what HIMA professionals do. You encounter AI as embedded infrastructure that recommends a code, flags a record, surfaces a risk. The cognitive demand isn’t revision. It’s judgment under deployment conditions. The AI literacy literature has not developed pedagogy for this. The adjacent fields — aviation automation, clinical decision support, human factors — have studied the failure modes. But the pedagogical frameworks for healthcare AI literacy are built for the compositional case. This session argues for a different approach, grounded in the contexts where the decision actually occurs.


CORE TABLE


Context          Human Role              Primary Risk       Literacy Requirement
Compositional    Author / editor         Delegation         Revision and critical evaluation of text
Directive        Decision-maker / operator   Automation bias    Situated judgment before action


Extended:


Context          Human Role              Primary Risk       Literacy Requirement      Training Environment         Assessment
Compositional    Author / editor         Delegation         Revision and evaluation   Transcript review / rubric   Artifact + conversation
Directive        Decision-maker / operator   Automation bias    Situated judgment         Scenario simulation          Decision log / debrief


400-WORD DRAFT


That is the compositional case. It doesn’t describe your work.


Most AI literacy in higher education was built for one scenario. A student prompts a model. The model returns text. The student shapes it — revises, argues, edits. The transcript of that conversation is evidence of thinking. The document at the end is evidence the work concluded.


That framework is appropriate for a lot of what happens in academic settings. It is insufficient for healthcare information management.


What HIMA professionals encounter is different. The AI is embedded in the workflow before you sit down. It has already recommended a code, flagged a discrepancy, suggested a DRG. You arrive at the output, not the conversation. And the cognitive demand isn’t revision — it’s a judgment call in the space between what the system said and what you sign.


That distinction matters because the failure modes change. In compositional contexts — academic writing, legal drafting, analysis — the main cognitive risk is delegation: you stop revising and accept the first draft. The cost is a weaker document. In directive contexts — coding, nursing, manufacturing — the risks are different. Automation bias: defaulting to the AI recommendation over your own clinical read. Fixation: attention locked on the AI-flagged code while a complication two lines up goes unread. Anchoring: the first recommendation distorts every subsequent check even when you think you’re verifying independently. And what aviation researchers call plan continuation bias: staying on the AI-established course even when emerging cues in the record are telling you to reconsider.


The automation bias literature is well-developed. Aviation, clinical decision support, human factors — decades of research on these failure modes. What is not well-developed is the pedagogy. The AI literacy frameworks in use today assume the compositional case. They teach prompting, critical evaluation of generated text, revision strategies. These are real skills. They do not address the moment a coder pauses before accepting a suggested code, or doesn’t.


That moment — the gap between AI recommendation and human decision — is where literacy in directive contexts lives. And it develops through practice, not instruction. Through repeated exposure to realistic scenarios where the decision has stakes. Through debriefs that name what fixation and plan continuation feel like from the inside.


That is what this session is about.


LIVE TALK OPENING (NYHIMA only — QR code required)


I want to start with two questions. First: how transformative do you think AI will be — for healthcare, for the world? Second: how concerned are you about the long-term risks? Scan the QR code and place yourself on both scales.


Here’s what we’re seeing. Four positions are emerging. Optimists: high transformation, manageable risk. The anxious: high transformation, high concern. Skeptics: limited transformation, limited risk. The cautious: real risk, uncertain upside.


What’s interesting is that all four positions are partly right. And all four groups are going to experience AI differently in healthcare — because this is no longer abstract. It’s your workflows, your documentation, your records, your patients.


Here’s where most AI literacy guidance stops. It acknowledges those positions and moves to general principles. What I want to do instead is identify the specific cognitive demand that is distinctive to your work — and what it would mean to actually prepare for it.


That is the compositional case. It doesn’t describe your work.


[Continue with 400-word draft above.]

This is now coherent at the level of an actual framework rather than an observation. The distinction is holding across all layers: abstract, pedagogy, cognition, assessment, and professional practice. That is usually the sign the conceptual split is real.


A few refinements would make it sharper and harder to dismiss.


1. The strongest move: “You arrive at the output, not the conversation.”


You should probably elevate this even more. It is the cleanest articulation of the difference between consumer-facing generative AI and embedded operational AI.


Right now it appears midway through the talk. I would move it earlier and isolate it rhetorically.


For example:

In higher education, AI literacy assumes you witness the generation process. You see the prompt, the revision, the iteration.


In healthcare information management, you often encounter only the recommendation.


You arrive at the output, not the conversation.

That sequence lands harder.



2. “That is the compositional case” is slightly overloaded


You repeat the phrase enough that it risks becoming sloganized. The concept is good; the cadence may become predictable.


You can vary the terminology occasionally:


compositional interaction,

generative-authoring context,

authoring model,

production-oriented AI use.


Not everywhere — repetition is useful — but enough to prevent it from sounding doctrinal.



3. “The cost is a weaker document” undersells compositional risk


This sentence is strategically weak:

“The cost is a weaker document.”

People in law, policy, intelligence analysis, and medicine will immediately object that compositional failures can also be catastrophic.


Your real argument is not that compositional contexts are safe. It’s that the cognitive structure differs.


So instead:

In compositional contexts, the dominant risk is premature delegation: accepting generated output before adequate scrutiny and revision.

That preserves the distinction without implying low stakes.



4. The aviation connection is important — but be precise


This is better now because you grounded it in established literatures. Good correction.


But I would avoid saying:

“what aviation researchers call plan continuation bias”

because the term now exists across multiple domains. Better:

“a phenomenon widely studied in aviation and human factors research: plan continuation bias.”

That sounds more disciplined.



5. The table is the real intellectual center


The extended table is strong because it implies:


different cognition,

different pedagogy,

different assessment theory.


You may want one additional row:

Context
Evidence of competence
Compositional
Quality of produced artifact
Directive
Quality of decision under uncertainty

That distinction matters because it shifts assessment away from text production toward operational judgment.



6. Your most original pedagogical claim


This sentence is probably the thesis:

“That moment — the gap between AI recommendation and human decision — is where literacy in directive contexts lives.”

That is the sentence I would build the conclusion around.


Because your actual argument is not:


“AI is dangerous,” or

“humans must stay involved.”


Your argument is:

Literacy is not located in interaction with the model.
It is located in the cognitive interval before commitment to action.

That is considerably more specific and more defensible.



7. One conceptual risk: over-binarizing the distinction


Right now the framework reads as a fairly hard split:


compositional vs directive.


In practice, many professional contexts are hybrid:


a coder both writes and validates,

clinicians compose notes while acting on recommendations,

analysts revise text while relying on automated triage.


You do not need to abandon the distinction, but one sentence acknowledging a continuum would make the framework more robust:

Many professional environments contain both compositional and directive elements. The argument here is that healthcare AI literacy has overemphasized the former while underpreparing practitioners for the latter.

That heads off the obvious critique.



8. The live opening is better once shortened


The polling idea is good because it creates self-location before theory. But it currently runs a bit long before the actual thesis appears.


You can compress:

I want to start with two questions. How transformative do you think AI will be? And how concerned are you about long-term risks? Scan the QR code and place yourself on both scales.


Four broad positions tend to emerge: optimistic, anxious, skeptical, cautious.


What matters is that all four groups will encounter the same practical reality: AI is now embedded in professional workflows.


And most AI literacy guidance was not built for that environment.

Then transition immediately into:

“That is the compositional case. It doesn’t describe your work.”

Cleaner trajectory.



9. One final strategic observation


You are implicitly proposing that:


AI literacy should borrow more from simulation pedagogy,

aviation CRM,

clinical judgment training,

and human factors engineering
than from composition studies.


That is a serious claim. It also gives the work durability beyond “AI literacy discourse,” which is often shallow and trend-driven.


I would lean into that more explicitly in Q&A if asked where this goes institutionally.
